title: The Case for Christian Fitness
author: Ad Aeternum
summary: In 'The Case for Christian Fitness,' the Ad Aeternum newsletter argues that physical training is a spiritual necessity for Christian men, not merely an optional lifestyle choice, because 'a strong body begets a strong mind and soul.' The author frames Christian life itself as a fight requiring endurance, and argues a fit body better equips a man to protect and serve the people who depend on him, to speak with credibility, and to embody the virtues of discipline and self-control he hopes to model. The piece identifies two common failure modes - neglecting fitness entirely as spiritually irrelevant, or pursuing it purely out of vanity - and argues both miss the point, since the goal is a body capable of serving others, not merely one that looks impressive. Its theological anchor is the Incarnation: because God took on a body to sanctify it as an instrument for holiness, neglecting one's own body is framed as a failure to take that doctrine seriously. The essay closes by explicitly subordinating fitness to the larger Christian mission of pursuing sanctity, warning against idolizing the body, while still insisting that fathers and husbands cannot afford a soft, weak body if they intend to fulfill their role.
points: The essay's central claim is theological rather than aesthetic: physical training matters because neglecting the body fails to take seriously the meaning of the Incarnation, which sanctified the body as an instrument for holiness.

It identifies two flawed extremes — disregarding fitness as spiritually irrelevant, or pursuing it purely for vanity and attraction — and argues a holistic approach trains the body to be functional and useful, not merely decorative.

Physical discipline is framed as instrumental to leadership and credibility: 'the messenger very often matters more than the message itself,' so a man preaching strength and discipline undermines his own message if his body doesn't embody it.

The piece explicitly subordinates fitness to a larger mission — pursuing sanctity and furthering God's Kingdom — warning against idolizing the body even while insisting fitness is necessary for fathers and husbands.
quotes: Christian life is a fight. We struggle against our sins, against endless temptations, against the natural suffering of life, and seek standards of excellence that are just short of impossible.
The fact of the matter is that a strong body begets a strong mind and soul. That means a fit, strong man will likely develop strength of spirit and will too.
The messenger very often matters more than the message itself. If you want people to take you seriously, you need to embody your philosophy with every fiber of your being.

It's important to note that physical training and being physically fit is a necessary pursuit, but it shouldn't be the central one for a Christian man. Our mission is to pursue sanctity and perfection under Christ, and further God's Kingdom on earth.

The Christian man who neglects his body has not really paid attention to the meaning of the Incarnation. God did not take on flesh as something secondary and meaningless, but to sanctify the body, and make it an instrument for holiness.
If you're truly aiming to fulfill your role as a father and husband properly, you simply cannot afford the luxury of a soft, weak body.
